input: A temperature loop holds the vessel temperature at the set point by acting on the heating supply, and the loop is built from a sensor, a controller and a final element, closed by the sign of the feedback. The sensor measures the vessel temperature. A temperature element immersed in the vessel contents produces a signal that follows the temperature, and this signal is all the loop knows of the controlled variable: a sensor in a stagnant pocket reports the pocket, and the loop controls the pocket temperature, not the vessel temperature. The controller compares the temperature with the set point and forms the error, the difference between the two. From the sign and size of the error, the controller sets the direction and amount of the correction: a temperature below the set point calls for more heating, and one above it calls for less. The controller moves nothing in the process itself; its output is a signal, and the signal carries no power. The final element turns the signal into a change in the process. The final element is the control valve in the heating line: the valve opens or closes on the controller signal, the flow of heating medium changes, and the changed flow moves the vessel temperature. The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in temperature above the set point produces a correction that reduces the heating, and a fall produces a correction that increases it, so the loop acts against the deviation that produced the correction. Connected with the opposite sign, the loop would act with the deviation and drive the temperature away from the set point, and no controller setting would make it control.
